# 1.2 - Factors, Multiples & Prime Factorization {.unnumbered}

Have you ever had to split something up evenly, like slices of pizza or players on a team? That’s really what {{< glink slug="factor" text="factors" >}} are about: dividing numbers into equal parts.

In this lesson, you’ll learn how to:

  - Spot factors and {{< glink slug="multiple" text="multiples" >}}.

  - Tell if a number is {{< glink "prime number" >}} or {{< glink "composite number" >}}.

  - Break numbers into their basic building blocks using a {{< glink "factor tree" >}}.

You’ll use these skills again and again, from simplifying fractions to solving equations.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I can find the factors and multiples of integers
- [ ] I can tell if a number is prime or composite
- [ ] I can break numbers into prime factors using a factor tree
:::

{{< warmup >}}

1. How many different pairs of whole numbers can you multiply to get 36?

2. How many whole numbers can you multiply by 7 and still get a result less than 50?

3. Can you find more than one pair of whole numbers that multiply to make 13? 

{{< learn >}}

### 1.2.1 - What Are Factors?

A {{< glink factor >}} of a number is a whole number that divides it evenly (with no {{< glink remainder >}}).

**Example 1:** Factors of 12

The factors of 12 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12

That’s because:

1 × 12 = 12

2 × 6 = 12

3 × 4 = 12

:::{.think title="Can a number have just one factor?"}
Only one number does: **1**. It only has itself as a factor!
:::

***

### 1.2.2 - What Are Multiples?

A {{< glink multiple >}} is what you get when you multiply a number by a whole number.

So the multiples of 5 are $5 \times 1$, $5 \times 2$, $5 \times 3$, and so on.

**Example 2:** Multiples of 5

Here are the first few multiples of 5: 

$5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, ...$

**Where have we seen this before?**

Multiples show up all over the place. When you {{< glink "skip count" >}}, you are using multiples. In the previous lesson, we used multiples to construct number lines! 

They show up outside of math class too. If a bus comes every 15 minutes, the arrival times are multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60…

***

**Example 3:** Multiples of 3

Here is a number line that shows multiples of three.
![](/images/Unit_1/Lesson_2/skip_count_by_3.png)

### 1.2.3 - Prime vs. Composite

Some numbers can only be divided evenly two ways, others can be broken into many parts. Let's explore the difference between {{< glink slug="prime-number" text="prime numbers" >}} and {{< glink slug="composite-number" text="composite numbers" >}}.

A **prime number** has only 2 factors: 1 and itself.

Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13...

A **composite number** has more than 2 factors.

Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10...

The number 1 is **neither** prime nor composite. It has only one factor — itself — so it does not have the 2 factors a prime needs, and it does not have more than 2 either.

:::{.real-world}
People around the world spend years searching for giant prime numbers. The largest ones we’ve found so far have over 24 million digits!

Why go to all that trouble?

Prime numbers are the secret behind modern encryption. They're used to protect everything from bank accounts to private messages. The bigger the primes, the harder they are to break. That's why finding huge ones is such a big deal.

It’s like a global math scavenger hunt… with real-world consequences.
:::

***

### 1.2.4 - Prime Factorization and Factor Trees

Every number can be broken into a {{< glink product >}} of prime numbers. These prime factors are the basic building blocks of all whole numbers.

We use **factor trees** to find these prime factors. This isn’t just a fun trick, it builds your {{< glink "number sense" >}}, your ability to see patterns, understand how numbers are structured, and work confidently with them.

That number sense will come in handy later when you:

* Simplify fractions
* Solve equations
* Factor algebraic expressions

Let’s build a factor tree for **360** to see how it works.

***

#### Steps to Make a Factor Tree

1. Start with a number: 

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
```
</div>
<br>
2. Find any two numbers that multiply to give the number: $360 = 18 \times 20$

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
    node_1_0_1("18")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_1_1("20")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
```
</div>
<br>
3. Break each of those numbers down further:

   - $18 = 3 \times 6$
   - $20 = 4 \times 5$

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
    node_1_0_1("18")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_0_2_0_2("3")
    node_1_0_1 --- node_1_0_2_0_2
    node_1_0_2_1_2("6")
    node_1_0_1 --- node_1_0_2_1_2
    node_1_1_1("20")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
    node_1_1_2_0_2("4")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_0_2
    node_1_1_2_1_2("5")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_1_2
```
</div>
<br>
4. Keep going until all branches end in **prime numbers** (numbers that can’t be factored anymore, like 2, 3, 5, 7...). We call the ends of the branches "leaves".

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
    flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
    node_1_0_1("18")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_0_2_0_2("3")
    node_1_0_1 --- node_1_0_2_0_2
    node_1_0_2_1_2("6")
    node_1_0_1 --- node_1_0_2_1_2
    node_1_0_2_1_3_0_3("2")
    node_1_0_2_1_2 --- node_1_0_2_1_3_0_3
    node_1_0_2_1_3_1_3("3")
    node_1_0_2_1_2 --- node_1_0_2_1_3_1_3
    node_1_1_1("20")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
    node_1_1_2_0_2("4")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_0_2
    node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_0_2 --- node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3
    node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_0_2 --- node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3
    node_1_1_2_1_2("5")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_1_2

    style node_1_1_2_1_2 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_0_2_1_3_1_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_0_2_1_3_0_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_0_2_0_2 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;

```
</div>
<br>
5. The prime factorization is the product of the leaves of the tree: <br> 
$$2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 = 360$$
This can be written more compactly by using the factor counts as {{< glink slug="exponent" text="exponents" >}}. There are three 2s and two 3s in this case and so we get...<br>
$$2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$$

***

There are *many* factor trees for the number 360. For example, you could also have started with $360 = 3 \times 120$.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
    node_1_0_1("3")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_1_1("120")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
    node_1_1_2_0_2("2")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_0_2
    node_1_1_2_1_2("60")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_1_2
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3("15")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_0_4("5")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_0_4
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_1_4("3")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_1_4
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3("4")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4("2")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4("2")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4

    style node_1_0_1 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_2 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_1_4 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_0_4_0_4 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
```

</div>
<br>
There are still three 2s, two 3s, and one 5, so the prime factorization does not change!
$$2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$$
As long as you end up with the same prime numbers, the tree is correct!

***

:::{.note title="Which factors should I start with?"}

There is no one right answer to this question. It depends on your goal. If your goal is finding easy numbers, you might start small.  Notice that 360 is {{< glink even >}}, that means it is divisible by 2. We could divide by 2 and keep going that way.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("360")
    node_1_0_1("2")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_1_1("180")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
    node_1_1_2_0_2("2")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_0_2
    node_1_1_2_1_2("90")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_1_2
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3("45")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4("3")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4("15")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_0_5("3")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_0_5
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_1_5("5")
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_4 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_1_5

    style node_1_0_1 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_2 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_0_4 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_0_5 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_4_1_5_1_5 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
```
</div>

When you divide by the smallest (or biggest) factors, the tree tends to become deep. If you want smaller trees, you should start with factor pairs that are closer together like we did with the first factor tree for 360, splitting first with 18 and 20.

:::

**What About Negative Numbers?**

If the number is negative, factor out a -1 first. Here is one possible factor tree for -24:

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

```{mermaid}
%%| label: mermaid-diagram
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: " "
flowchart TB
    node_0("-24")
    node_1_0_1("-1")
    node_0 --- node_1_0_1
    node_1_1_1("24")
    node_0 --- node_1_1_1
    node_1_1_2_0_2("4")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_0_2
    node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_0_2 --- node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3
    node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_0_2 --- node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3
    node_1_1_2_1_2("6")
    node_1_1_1 --- node_1_1_2_1_2
    node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3("2")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3
    node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3("3")
    node_1_1_2_1_2 --- node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3

    style node_1_0_1 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_3_0_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_0_3_1_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_0_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
    style node_1_1_2_1_3_1_3 stroke-width:4px,font-weight:bold;
```
</div>
<br>

So, the prime factorization of -24 is...

$$-1 \times 2^3 \times 3 = -24$$


This will come in handy later when we factor algebraic {{< glink slug="expression" text="expressions" >}} like $-x^2 + 4x$. It’s often helpful to pull out a negative first!

**Feeling overwhelmed?**

If you struggle to come up with the factors for a number, you should check out the [factor chart](/resources/Factor-Chart_noprimes.pdf) in the resources section of this book. It shows all of the factor pairs for many composite numbers!
